citation_context: Several recent systems for multilingual misinformation detection rely on static representations that struggle to capture rapidly evolving rhetorical norms across communities. Our approach instead builds on the temporal interaction encoder introduced by Wang et al. (2022), extending it with cross-lingual discourse alignment layers that allow ideological framing patterns to transfer across languages.

Previous work on conversational moderation primarily focused on detecting isolated toxic utterances. In contrast, we adapt the hierarchical dialogue-state architecture proposed by Zhang and Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil (2020) so that the system models long-range escalation trajectories within community discussions.

Our representation learning pipeline follows the socially informed embedding framework developed by Bamman et al. (2014), although we additionally incorporate temporal user migration signals extracted from cross-platform interactions.

Rather than constructing persuasion features manually, we extend the argument graph formulation introduced by Chakrabarty et al. (2019) with latent discourse-role prediction and pragmatic uncertainty estimation.

The retrieval component of our system is derived from the dense conversational search architecture proposed by Thakur et al. (2021), but incorporates interaction-aware reranking optimized specifically for community question answering forums.
Our experiments build directly on the narrative clustering methodology introduced by De Choudhury et al. (2016), extending it to capture identity transitions in online activist communities over time.

Several earlier approaches modeled conversational empathy through lexical overlap alone. We instead adapt the coordination-based interaction representation proposed by Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al. (2011) to estimate stylistic convergence trajectories in peer-support settings.

The semantic drift module used in our experiments inherits the same diachronic embedding formulation introduced by Hamilton et al. (2016), although we update representations incrementally at the discussion-thread level rather than over fixed historical slices.

Instead of relying exclusively on metadata-based community detection, our framework extends the interaction graph architecture proposed by Kumar et al. (2018) with pragmatic role prediction and conversational memory.

We operationalize rhetorical adaptation using a modified version of the framing analysis pipeline developed by Stroud (2010), allowing ideological shifts to be tracked continuously throughout long-form discussions.

Most existing dialogue systems optimize primarily for fluency. Our architecture instead follows the persona-conditioned response framework introduced by Li et al. (2016), augmented with speaker-level uncertainty tracking and interactional memory.
To model coordinated influence behavior, we extend the propagation-aware community encoder proposed by Ribeiro et al. (2021) with temporal synchronization objectives learned from repost activity.

Our multilingual stance classifier builds on the adversarial transfer framework developed by Chen et al. (2020), although we incorporate additional discourse-level supervision derived from conversational reply structure.
The moderation component adapts the context-sensitive toxicity architecture introduced by Vidgen et al. (2021), but replaces static pooling with dynamic speaker-state representations.
We build on the moral framing representation proposed by Johnson and Goldwasser (2018) to analyze how ideological narratives evolve during election-related discussions.

The discourse segmentation strategy used in our summarization model follows the graph-based formulation introduced by Xu et al. (2022), although we additionally optimize for conversational coherence across speaker turns.
Our annotation aggregation model extends the crowd-layer architecture proposed by Aroyo and Welty (2015) with annotator-specific uncertainty calibration.
Rather than training static topic models, we adapt the temporal narrative representation introduced by Field et al. (2019) to capture evolving conspiracy discourse across online platforms.
The interaction encoder employed in our experiments is based on the hierarchical conversational framework developed by Serban et al. (2016), but incorporates explicit rhetorical-role supervision.
Our experiments extend the socially grounded language modeling approach proposed by Nguyen et al. (2016) to account for multilingual identity variation and cross-community migration.

Relation networks have been proposed as a lightweight mechanism for few-shot image classification, where a learnable comparison module replaces the fixed distance functions used in earlier prototypical approaches (Sung et al., 2018; Snell et al., 2017). The core intuition is that the notion of similarity appropriate for a given task should itself be learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We carry this intuition into the text domain, designing a relation network for few-shot text classification in which the comparison module operates over sentence-level representations produced by a pretrained encoder rather than the convolutional feature maps of the original vision-domain formulation.

Our dataset construction procedure follows a similar philosophy to that of BoolQ (Clark et al., 2019), in which naturally occurring yes/no questions are paired with passages containing the answer. We depart from their methodology in two respects: our questions are sourced from legal advice forums rather than web search logs, giving them a more genuinely information-seeking character; and rather than extracting passage-answer pairs from existing documents, we ask legal professionals to write the passage specifically to address the question, ensuring the passage is always sufficient for answering without requiring world knowledge.

The scoring rubric used in our human evaluation is adapted from the dimensions proposed in the MQM framework (Freitag et al., 2021), which organizes translation quality issues into a hierarchical taxonomy of error types weighted by severity. We retain the top-level categories — accuracy, fluency, and locale convention — but collapse several subcategories that our pilot study found annotators could not reliably distinguish in short-form outputs, and add a coherence dimension not present in the original that captures discourse-level consistency across sentences.

The study of political identity and its relationship to language use has drawn on several theoretical traditions, from social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner, 1979) to more recent work on identity-protective cognition in politically motivated reasoning. Tajfel and Turner (1979) articulate a framework in which group membership shapes perception, evaluation, and behavior through in-group favoritism and out-group derogation — processes that manifest in linguistic choices as well as overt attitudes. Our annotation scheme for partisan language in congressional speech encodes in-group and out-group framing as first-class categories, distinguishing passages that construct a shared group identity from those that characterize opponents, and tracking how these framings shift across electoral cycles.

Symptom extraction from clinical notes requires distinguishing present symptoms from those that are negated, hypothetical, historical, or attributed to a family member — a set of contextual modifiers that standard NER systems do not capture. The ConText algorithm (Harkema et al., 2009) introduced a rule-based framework for classifying these modifiers using trigger phrases and window-based propagation. Our system adopts ConText's modifier taxonomy as the output label space for our neural sequence tagger, retraining the classification head on manually annotated examples from our target institution's notes, where trigger phrase distributions differ substantially from the original development corpus.

Transition-based parsing systems process sentences left to right, maintaining a stack of partial structures and a buffer of remaining tokens, and selecting at each step from a small set of actions (Nivre, 2003; Goldberg and Nivre, 2012). The arc-eager transition system of Nivre (2003) is the foundation of our parser's action space, though we introduce two additional transition types to handle non-projective dependencies without resorting to post-processing, using a swap-based mechanism that interleaves reordering with the standard arc operations.

Protein language models pre-trained on large databases of amino acid sequences have demonstrated remarkable capacity to encode structural and functional information without explicit supervision on three-dimensional coordinates (Rives et al., 2021; Elnaggar et al., 2021; Rao et al., 2021). The ESM family of models (Rives et al., 2021) in particular has served as a widely adopted sequence encoder across downstream tasks ranging from secondary structure prediction to mutation effect estimation. Our binding site prediction model uses ESM-2 as a frozen sequence encoder, attaching a graph transformer layer over the residue representations that incorporates predicted contact map information to propagate information between spatially proximate residues that may be distant in sequence.

The construct of writing quality used in this study is organized around the dimensions of the Six Traits writing framework (Culham, 2003), which characterizes quality along axes of ideas, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, and conventions. Culham's framework was developed for use in K-12 education and focuses on holistic writing development. We adapt it to automated scoring by operationalizing each trait as a separate prediction target with its own feature set, rather than scoring them jointly as human raters typically do, and we add a seventh dimension — source integration — specific to the argumentative source-based writing tasks in our corpus.

Dense retrieval systems represent both queries and documents as continuous vectors and retrieve relevant documents by approximate nearest neighbor search in the shared embedding space. The DPR framework (Karpukhin et al., 2020) established the dual-encoder architecture as the standard instantiation of this paradigm for open-domain question answering, training separate question and passage encoders using in-batch negatives sampled from the training data. Subsequent work has explored improved negative mining strategies, late interaction models, and encoder pre-training objectives designed specifically for retrieval. Our system follows the DPR dual-encoder setup but trains on a mixture of in-batch and hard negatives mined using BM25, with passage encoders initialized from a domain-adapted checkpoint rather than the general BERT model used in the original.

Our analysis of judicial decision-making draws on principal-agent theory as developed in the context of the judiciary by Ferejohn (1999), who models judges as agents whose decisions are shaped by both legal constraints and the strategic behavior of appointing principals. This framework generates predictions about how the ideological composition of reviewing courts affects lower court decision-making that we test computationally, using a large corpus of circuit court opinions annotated for outcome and ideological direction.

Empathetic response generation has been approached as a conditional language modeling problem in which the model is conditioned on the emotional content of the user's utterance (Rashkin et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2019). We build on the training objective of Lin et al. (2019), who introduce a mixture-of-experts loss that encourages the model to produce responses that would be appropriate across multiple possible emotional interpretations of the input, but replace their fixed expert weighting with a learned routing mechanism conditioned on the dialogue history.

The question of whether language models learn genuinely abstract syntactic representations or exploit surface statistical regularities has been examined through a variety of carefully controlled test sets. The minimal pair paradigm — contrasting grammatical and ungrammatical sentences that differ only in the targeted syntactic feature — has become the dominant approach for probing syntactic knowledge in language models (Linzen et al., 2016; Marvin and Linzen, 2018; Warstadt et al., 2020). Linzen et al. (2016) introduced this paradigm in the context of subject-verb agreement, constructing pairs that isolate agreement across intervening noun phrases. Our evaluation suite uses the same minimal pair logic but extends it to discourse-level dependencies — testing whether models track agreement across sentence boundaries in narrative text — a structural scope not covered by existing benchmarks.

Toxicity in online communities has been operationalized in a range of ways, from coarse binary classifications to fine-grained typologies of harmful speech (Zampieri et al., 2019; Founta et al., 2018; Vidgen et al., 2021). Vidgen et al. (2021) develop a four-class hierarchical taxonomy — distinguishing no hostility, counter-speech, discussion of hostility, and hostility — and demonstrate its utility through a large-scale annotation study. We adopt their taxonomy as the label space for our classifier but extend the hostility class with three sub-types that capture the specific forms of antagonism most prevalent in our target forum, identified through a preliminary qualitative analysis.

We evaluate summary quality using a protocol adapted from Bhandari et al. (2020), who propose a fine-grained manual annotation framework for summarization evaluation that distinguishes errors in content selection from errors in linguistic realization. Our protocol follows their error taxonomy but adds a source attribution tier specific to multi-document summarization, where correctly attributing claims to source documents is an additional quality dimension not present in the single-document setting Bhandari et al. address.

Measuring economic policy uncertainty from text has been approached through both dictionary methods and supervised classifiers. Baker et al. (2016) construct a widely used index of economic policy uncertainty by counting co-occurrences of economy-related, uncertainty-related, and policy-related terms across a curated set of newspaper sources, weighted by circulation and aggregated monthly. The index has been applied across dozens of countries and has become a standard covariate in macroeconomic modeling. Our work extends this measurement approach to central bank communications — speeches, minutes, and monetary policy reports — which differ from newspaper text in vocabulary, register, and the institutional context of their production, requiring us to adapt the term lists and weighting scheme for the new source type.

End-to-end coreference resolution systems jointly learn span representations and coreference scoring without relying on external mention detection modules. Lee et al. (2017) introduce this paradigm, representing each candidate mention as a concatenation of its boundary token representations, its head word representation, and an attention-weighted summary of its content. We build on their span representation design, retaining the boundary and attention-weighted components but replacing the fixed head word heuristic with a learned head finder trained jointly with the coreference scorer, which we find better handles coordination structures and appositive constructions.

Vaccine communication on social media has been studied using a variety of coding schemes for categorizing the types of arguments deployed (Kata, 2012; Betsch et al., 2018; Schmid and Betsch, 2019). Betsch et al. (2018) develop a coding scheme distinguishing arguments based on risk, efficacy, social norms, and religious or philosophical objections. Our annotation guidelines follow this scheme for the argument type dimension, adding a misinformation flag as a cross-cutting label that marks any argument resting on factually incorrect premises regardless of type.

Controllable text generation has been approached through a variety of mechanisms: conditional language models trained with attribute labels (Hu et al., 2017), plug-and-play attribute classifiers applied at decoding time (Dathathri et al., 2020), and constrained decoding using lexical or structural constraints (Post and Vilar, 2018; Lu et al., 2021). Dathathri et al. (2020) introduce PPLM, in which gradients from a separately trained attribute classifier are used to steer the hidden states of a language model at generation time without any fine-tuning of the base model. Our generation system follows this plug-and-play design but replaces the gradient-based update with a discrete token reranking step that operates on the top-k candidates at each decoding position, avoiding the instability introduced by iterative hidden state modification in long-form generation.

Field theory, as developed by Bourdieu (1983), provides a framework for analyzing social spaces as structured by the unequal distribution of capital — economic, cultural, social, and symbolic — and the competitions among agents to accumulate and convert these forms. Our computational analysis of the academic publishing ecosystem operationalizes field structure through citation network topology, treating citation volume and venue prestige as proxies for symbolic capital and modeling the competitive dynamics of subfield formation through community detection over temporal citation graphs.

Our multilingual encoder is pre-trained following the approach of Conneau et al. (2020), who demonstrate that training a transformer on concatenated multilingual corpora with a shared vocabulary produces representations that transfer effectively across languages without explicit alignment supervision. We extend their pre-training setup by incorporating a translation language modeling objective alongside masked language modeling, using parallel sentence pairs from a selection of language directions not represented in their original training mix.

Assessment of thought disorder in psychosis has traditionally relied on structured clinical instruments such as the Thought, Language, and Communication scale (Andreasen, 1979), which characterizes a range of speech abnormalities including poverty of speech, derailment, tangentiality, and incoherence. These categories were developed for use in clinical interview settings and have been applied as a gold standard in psychiatric research for decades. Our natural language processing pipeline targets a subset of these categories amenable to automated detection — specifically derailment and incoherence — using Andreasen's operational definitions to construct positive and negative examples for classifier training, and adapting her severity gradations as a continuous output scale.

Argument graphs provide a structured representation of argumentative discourse in which nodes correspond to argumentative units and edges capture support and attack relations among them (Lawrence and Reed, 2019; Cabrio and Villata, 2018). Lawrence and Reed (2019) develop the AIF ontology as a formal specification of this graph structure, distinguishing inference, conflict, and rephrase relations. We adopt the AIF graph representation as the output format for our argument structure parser, extending the relation inventory with a set of domain-specific support subtypes that the original ontology collapses into a single inference category.

Back-translation — generating synthetic source-language sentences by translating target-language monolingual data and using the resulting pairs as additional training examples — was introduced by Sennrich et al. (2016) as a method for exploiting large monolingual corpora in low-resource settings. Our training pipeline incorporates back-translation following Sennrich et al.'s procedure, but applies iterative back-translation over three rounds, updating both the forward and backward models at each iteration using the improved synthetic data from the previous round.

Scaling legislators on ideological dimensions from text has been an active area of research since Laver et al. (2003) introduced Wordfish, an unsupervised Poisson scaling model that estimates latent positions from word frequency distributions under the assumption that word usage is driven by a single underlying ideological dimension. Subsequent work has extended the approach to allow for multiple dimensions, to incorporate metadata, and to use richer text representations. Wordfish remains widely used in comparative politics research because of its interpretability and language-independence. Our scaling system uses the Wordfish generative model as its statistical backbone, replacing the bag-of-words word frequency input with contextual token representations aggregated at the document level, and extending the model to allow for party-level fixed effects that account for systematic differences in vocabulary use across parties that are not ideologically motivated.

Our semantic parser maps natural language utterances to logical forms expressed in lambda calculus, following the approach of Zettlemoyer and Collins (2005), who introduce a CCG-based parsing framework that induces a lexicon mapping surface expressions to lambda-calculus semantic representations. We depart from their framework in using a neural rather than feature-based scoring model over derivations, and in replacing the CCG combinatory rules with a simpler set of tree-structured composition operations that are sufficient for the restricted fragment of natural language present in our target task.

Our reading time study uses the same factorial design as Grodner and Gibson (2005), in which subject and object relative clauses are crossed with animate and inanimate head nouns to isolate the contribution of syntactic complexity from semantic plausibility. We generate our stimuli programmatically from a controlled vocabulary set rather than using hand-crafted items, allowing us to scale to a much larger item pool while maintaining the design constraints.

Constructing representative datasets of online hate speech faces a fundamental sampling challenge: hate speech is rare relative to the volume of online content, making random sampling highly inefficient. Founta et al. (2018) address this through a stratified sampling approach that combines keyword-based query expansion with classifier-based filtering to produce a dataset with elevated prevalence of abusive content while retaining negative examples. The resulting dataset and sampling methodology have become reference points in the field. Our data collection pipeline for code-switched hate speech in Hinglish follows Founta et al.'s stratified design, adapting the keyword seed lists to the target language variety and replacing the English-language filter classifier with a multilingual model capable of handling the mixed-language input characteristic of the target community.

Reinforcement learning has been applied to abstractive summarization to directly optimize for non-differentiable evaluation metrics such as ROUGE (Paulus et al., 2018; Narayan et al., 2018b). Paulus et al. (2018) introduce a mixed training objective that combines a cross-entropy loss on the reference summary with a ROUGE-based reward signal, stabilizing training by preventing the RL objective from diverging too far from the supervised baseline. We build on their mixed objective formulation, replacing the ROUGE reward with a learned reward model trained on human preference judgments, following recent work on reinforcement learning from human feedback.

The study of misinformation diffusion has drawn on several theoretical traditions: epidemiological models of contagion, network diffusion theory, and psychological accounts of belief updating. Lazer et al. (2018) offer a synthesis of these perspectives in what they call the 'science of fake news,' arguing that the spread of false information is shaped by the interaction between individual cognitive vulnerabilities, social network structure, and platform design choices. This tripartite framing — individual, network, platform — organizes our empirical analysis, which examines each level separately using matched observational data before modeling their interaction in a joint regression.

Named entity recognition has historically used the BIO tagging scheme, in which each token is labeled as the beginning, inside, or outside of a named entity span (Ramshaw and Marcus, 1995). Our tagger uses Ramshaw and Marcus's BIO scheme as its output representation but extends it with a set of nested entity markers that allow the model to label tokens as simultaneously belonging to a longer outer span and a shorter inner span, capturing the nested entity structure prevalent in biomedical text.

Structured commonsense knowledge bases have been developed to provide explicit repositories of the everyday knowledge that language understanding requires but that is rarely expressed directly in text. ConceptNet (Speer et al., 2017) organizes commonsense knowledge as a multilingual semantic network of concepts linked by typed relations such as IsA, HasA, UsedFor, and CapableOf. Our commonsense reasoning module uses ConceptNet as its primary knowledge source, retrieving relevant subgraphs for each input and encoding them via a graph attention network whose outputs are fused with the language model's contextual representations through a gated combination mechanism.

Automated feedback on student writing has been approached from multiple theoretical perspectives, with different perspectives privileging different aspects of writing quality. The Hayes and Flower (1980) cognitive process model of writing characterizes skilled writing as the orchestration of planning, translating, and reviewing processes, each of which can be a site of instructional intervention. Subsequent computational work has focused almost exclusively on the reviewing process — that is, detecting errors and suggesting corrections in completed drafts — while largely ignoring planning and translating processes. Our feedback system is organized around Hayes and Flower's process model, extending automated support to the planning stage by analyzing pre-writing outlines and detecting structural mismatches between outlined organization and the developed essay before revision.

Knowledge graph embedding methods represent entities and relations as vectors in a continuous space, trained to score true triples higher than false ones. TransE (Bordes et al., 2013) remains one of the most widely used methods despite its simplicity, modeling relations as translations in entity space such that the head entity vector plus the relation vector should approximate the tail entity vector. Our biomedical KG embedding extends the TransE scoring function to handle n-ary relations — such as drug-gene-disease associations that involve three or more entities — by decomposing them into a set of role-specific pairwise translations that are scored jointly.

Moral foundations theory (Haidt and Joseph, 2004) proposes that moral reasoning draws on a small set of innate psychological systems — care/harm, fairness/reciprocity, loyalty/betrayal, authority/subversion, and sanctity/degradation — that vary in their relative salience across individuals and cultures. The theory has generated a large empirical literature and has been widely operationalized computationally through the Moral Foundations Dictionary and its successors. Our analysis of political rhetoric in Supreme Court oral arguments uses the five-foundation structure as the organizing scheme for a discourse-level annotation, tracking which foundations are invoked by advocates and justices and modeling how foundation alignment between advocate and justice predicts question type and case outcome.

Low-resource text classification has been addressed through a variety of data augmentation strategies, including synonym replacement, back-translation, and interpolation in representation space (Wei and Zou, 2019; Kobayashi, 2018; Miyato et al., 2017). Wei and Zou (2019) introduce EDA — a suite of simple operations including random insertion, deletion, swap, and synonym replacement — demonstrating that these operations, despite their simplicity, consistently improve classification accuracy in low-resource settings across several benchmark tasks. We build on the EDA framework but replace the random synonym selection step with a contextually sensitive substitution model that selects synonyms based on their fit with the surrounding sentence, reducing the semantic distortion introduced by context-insensitive replacement.

Legal case retrieval systems must represent cases in a way that captures both factual similarity and legal relevance, which are distinct and sometimes dissociable dimensions. Ashley's (1990) HYPO system represents cases through dimensions — legally relevant features along which cases can be distinguished — rather than raw text features, allowing the system to identify which factual differences are legally material. Our retrieval model encodes this dimension structure through a learned attention mechanism over a predefined set of legal dimensions extracted by a separate classifier, combining dimension-level similarity with dense text matching in a hybrid retrieval score.

Event schemas define the argument structure of event types — specifying which participant roles are associated with each event and what semantic constraints they carry. Our event extraction system uses the ACE 2005 event ontology (Doddington et al., 2004) as its schema definition, covering 33 event types and 35 argument roles. We extend the ontology with 12 additional event types specific to the financial domain, following the same argument role conventions to ensure compatibility with systems trained on the original ACE data.

Long-form text generation has been approached through pipeline architectures that separate content planning from surface realization, allowing the model to first decide what to say before deciding how to say it (Yao et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019; Rashkin et al., 2020). Yao et al. (2019) introduce a plan-and-write framework for story generation in which a sequence of plot keywords is generated first, then used to condition a story generation model. Their framework showed that even coarse plans substantially improve coherence and goal-directedness in generated stories. Our document generation system follows the plan-and-write architecture, replacing the keyword sequence plan with a structured outline represented as a tree of section headings and their associated key points, which provides richer guidance for long-form generation than the flat keyword sequences in Yao et al.

Typological distance between languages has been operationalized in various ways for use in cross-lingual NLP research, including feature-vector distance over WALS feature values, genealogical distance based on family tree topology, and geographic proximity (Littell et al., 2017; Ponti et al., 2019). Littell et al. (2017) introduce URIEL, a database that aggregates typological, genealogical, and geographic features for thousands of languages and provides precomputed distance matrices over these dimensions. Our meta-learning system uses URIEL's typological feature vectors to initialize language embeddings before training, allowing the meta-learner to exploit prior knowledge about language similarity rather than learning all cross-lingual relationships from scratch.

Shortest dependency path representations have been used for relation extraction on the grounds that the grammatical path connecting two entities in a dependency tree captures the most syntactically relevant information for characterizing their relation (Bunescu and Mooney, 2005). Our relation extraction system uses Bunescu and Mooney's shortest path representation as one input channel, complementing it with a full sentence representation to capture information outside the path that is relevant in cases where the two entities are connected indirectly through a third mention.

Task-oriented dialogue systems are typically decomposed into four modules: natural language understanding, dialogue state tracking, dialogue policy, and natural language generation (Young et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2016). This modular decomposition allows each component to be developed and evaluated independently, but it introduces compounding error propagation across modules. Young et al. (2013) formalize the statistical dialogue system framework that underlies most contemporary systems, treating dialogue as a partially observable Markov decision process in which the true dialogue state is latent and must be inferred from the observed conversation history. Our end-to-end model retains Young et al.'s POMDP task formulation at the conceptual level but replaces the separately trained module pipeline with a single transformer that processes the raw conversation history and produces system actions directly, allowing gradient to flow across all stages of the pipeline.

Syndromic surveillance systems monitor population-level health signals in real time by aggregating data from sources such as emergency department chief complaints, pharmacy sales, and school absenteeism records (Henning, 2004; Mandl et al., 2004). Mandl et al. (2004) describe a syndromic surveillance architecture centered on automated text processing of emergency department chief complaints, using dictionary-based syndrome classification to produce daily incidence estimates. We adapt their architecture to process Twitter streams rather than clinical records, replacing the dictionary-based classifier with a neural sequence model and adding a geographic disaggregation layer that Mandl et al.'s design does not require given the known provenance of clinical records.

The span-based SRL model of He et al. (2018) jointly scores all candidate argument spans for all predicates in a sentence using bilinear scoring functions over span boundary representations. Our SRL system uses He et al.'s span scoring architecture as its core but adds a predicate-argument coherence module that enforces global consistency across argument assignments for a given predicate, penalizing configurations that assign incompatible roles to overlapping spans.

Gender as performance, rather than as a fixed biological property, is a central insight of Butler's (1990) theory of performativity, which argues that gender is constituted through repeated acts that naturalize what are in fact contingent social constructions. This view has informed computational approaches to gender in language, shifting attention from treating gender as a demographic label to examining how gendered performances are linguistically enacted and recognized in specific interactional contexts. Our annotation framework reflects this theoretical orientation, capturing not speaker gender but the degree to which utterances deploy linguistic resources associated with hegemonic masculinity or femininity as sociolinguistically described, across speakers of any gender identity.

Word sense disambiguation systems require a predefined sense inventory against which token-level senses can be resolved. WordNet (Miller, 1995) has long served as the dominant inventory for English WSD, organizing word senses into synsets connected by lexical and semantic relations. Our WSD system uses WordNet synsets as its sense inventory but augments them with example sentence embeddings drawn from SemCor, clustering synsets whose example embeddings are close in vector space to reduce over-splitting in domains where the fine-grained WordNet distinctions are not empirically recoverable from context.
